2How Many Pardons Does Each President Grant?

Presidents can forgive a federal crime or shorten a sentence on their own. See what the offenses were and when in a term the grants came.

Clemency grants per fiscal year

Context: Biden signed group commutation warrants for 1,499 people on Dec 12, 2024 and 2,490 on Jan 17, 2025; Trump’s Jan 20, 2025 proclamation covered about 1,500 January 6 defendants. All three fall in fiscal 2025’s peak. [DOJ, Federal Register]

Data notes

Grants counted from clemency warrants by the Justice Department’s Office of the Pardon Attorney, fiscal 1993 to January 2025, then counted from its list of Trump’s grants. “Group” means Biden’s two warrants (DOJ’s count), the January 6 proclamation (about 1,500, a reported figure with no official count) and the 2020 election proclamation (77 named). Numbered markers 1 and 2 are Biden’s marijuana proclamations, which DOJ doesn’t count, so they are not in the bars. Fiscal 1993 counts from Clinton’s first day, leaving out George H.W. Bush’s 38 grants that year. Clinton’s first grants came in fiscal 1995. Report a correction

President by president

Grants by president

Biden’s 4,245 grants are the most of any president shown, with 3,989 on two group warrants. Trump has about 1,750 through October 2026, about 1,580 of them by proclamation.

Data notes

Same counts as the chart above, by the president who signed. Per year divides by months in office, and Trump’s second term is still under way. DOJ’s figures back to 1900 show no larger total; Franklin Roosevelt’s 3,307 comes closest. Report a correction

What happened to petitions

Presidents granted 9% of decided petitions under Clinton, 2% under George W. Bush, 7% under Obama and 3% in Trump’s first term, when 8,123 closed without action and 180 were denied. Biden’s 15% includes his group warrants.

Data notes

Grants as a share of grants, denials and petitions closed without presidential action (a death, a release, or another administrative reason). A grant to someone who never petitioned still counts as granted, so this runs high for presidents who went around the office: of Trump’s 238 first-term grants, 129 applied through it, per DOJ. DOJ hasn’t published these figures for the current term. Report a correction

What for, and when

What the offenses were

Drug offenses were 90% of Obama’s individually listed grants and 65% of Biden’s. In Trump’s second term they are 17%, behind fraud and financial crimes at 27%.

Data notes

Each grant takes the category of the first offense listed. Biden’s 3,989 group grants and the proclamations have no listed offense here. Other includes military, Clean Air Act and clinic-access convictions. Mock only: categories are keyword rules; the build would use a checked classifier like the executive orders’. When in the term

Biden made 96% of his grants in his last 90 days and Trump 82% in his first term’s. In Trump’s second term, 97% through October 2026 came in the first year, most of them January 6 grants.

Share of each president’s grants by date, including group warrants and the January 6 and 2020 election proclamations. Trump’s second term is unfinished. Dates come from DOJ’s recipient lists. Report a correction

Years from sentence to pardon

The median pardon in Trump’s second term came 2 years after sentencing, through October 2026. From Clinton through Biden, each president’s median is between 12 and 24 years.

    Frequently asked questions

    What an executive order is

    What is the difference between an executive order and a law?

    A law is a statute enacted by Congress. An executive order is a written directive in which the President sets policy, and such orders tend to be directed to government officials. To have legal effect, an order must rest on the President's powers under the Constitution or on power Congress has delegated, and it cannot override a statute.

    Source: Congressional Research Service, Executive Orders: An Introduction

    Who writes executive orders?

    An agency official or other executive officer usually writes the first draft, which can start with a request from the President or with a proposal from an agency. Under the standing procedure, the draft goes to the Office of Management and Budget, which shares it with interested agencies for comment. It then goes to the Attorney General, whose Office of Legal Counsel reviews it for form and legality, and then to the President, who decides whether to sign. Not every order follows this process.

    Source: Congressional Research Service, Executive Orders: An Introduction

    Executive orders: limits and reach

    Who can overturn an executive order?

    A President can amend or revoke an executive order, and a later President can generally revoke or modify any earlier order. Congress can nullify the legal effect of an order that was issued under power Congress delegated to the President. Courts can also review an order and hold it unconstitutional when the President had no authority for it, either from the Constitution or from Congress.

    Source: Congressional Research Service, Executive Orders: An Introduction

    Who has to follow an executive order?

    Executive orders tend to be directed toward government officials, so the officials and agencies of the executive branch are the ones an order directs. Some orders are effective only against federal agencies or people acting as their officers, agents, or employees. Agency action that implements an order can also affect outside parties, who can challenge that action in court.

    Source: Congressional Research Service, Executive Orders: An Introduction

    Executive orders: counts

    Who signed the most executive orders?

    Franklin D. Roosevelt signed the most executive orders, with a total of 3,726 over 12.12 years in office. The table counts executive orders only, not memoranda or other written presidential directives.

    Source: The American Presidency Project (UC Santa Barbara), Executive Orders

    Pardons and commutations

    What is the difference between a pardon, a commutation and a group grant?

    A pardon is the President's forgiveness for a federal offense. It doesn't mean the person was innocent, and it can remove unpaid or unserved parts of a sentence. A commutation reduces a sentence being served, in full or in part, and leaves the conviction in place. "Group grant" is this page's label, not a legal term: one warrant or proclamation covering many people at once, such as Biden's commutation of 1,499 people on December 12, 2024 or Trump's January 6 proclamation. A group grant can be either a pardon or a commutation.

    Source: U.S. Department of Justice, Office of the Pardon Attorney, Frequently Asked Questions · U.S. Department of Justice, Commutations Granted by President Biden · Federal Register, Proclamation 10887

    Does a pardon erase a conviction?

    No. The Justice Department says a pardon does not signify innocence and that a pardoned offense stays on the person's record. Expungement is a separate remedy that courts rarely grant.

    Source: U.S. Department of Justice, Office of the Pardon Attorney, Frequently Asked Questions

    Can someone be pardoned before being convicted?

    Yes. The Justice Department says the President can pardon people who have not yet been convicted.

    Source: U.S. Department of Justice, Office of the Pardon Attorney, Frequently Asked Questions

    Pardon limits and process

    Can a president pardon state crimes?

    No. The Constitution gives the power over offenses against the United States, except in cases of impeachment. State convictions go to the authorities of that state.

    Source: National Archives, The Constitution, Article II, Section 2 · U.S. Department of Justice, Office of the Pardon Attorney, Frequently Asked Questions

    Does the president have to follow the Justice Department's advice?

    No. The Justice Department's clemency rules are advisory, for the internal guidance of its staff, and give applicants no enforceable rights. The President decides applications, apart from certain administrative closures.

    Source: U.S. Department of Justice, Office of the Pardon Attorney, Frequently Asked Questions

    Pardon counts

    Which president has granted the most clemency?

    Among presidents since Clinton, Biden has the most at 4,245, of which 3,989 were on two group warrants. Justice Department figures back to 1900 show no larger total; Franklin Roosevelt's 3,307 comes closest.

    Source: U.S. Department of Justice, Clemency Statistics
